summary: Shanghai AI Laboratory authors present Harness-of-Harness (HoH), a meta-harness that wraps existing coding-agent CLIs (Codex, OpenCode, Pi) in iterative planner-developer-tester loops. Each role returns schema-checked artifacts; state is persisted on disk behind an index (progressive disclosure); testing is separated from implementation; and project history is versioned. On sampled subsets of GameCraft-Bench (45 tasks), FrontierSWE (15) and ProgramBench, HoH@3 beats one-pass vanilla for all three harness-model pairs. A pass-matched control and three ablations are included, plus a 70-loop autonomous FPS-game case study.

claims.claim: HoH@3 outperforms the standalone harness for all three harness-model pairs on all three benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Table 1: GameCraft Overall 49.58->71.52 (Codex/GPT-5.5), 26.90->48.98 (OpenCode/DeepSeek-V4-Pro), 42.16->58.78 (Pi/MiniMax-M3); FrontierSWE dominance 44->71%, 25->44%, 35->64%; ProgramBench pass rate 60.41->66.50, 45.27->57.56, 35.83->52.68. Consistent direction, but one run per task-condition with provider-default sampling and no generation seed (App. B.2). Vanilla is a single pass against three for HoH, so this table does not control for compute.

claims.claim: Average relative gain 52.25%, max 82.86% after three iterations.
claims.evidence: These figures appear only in the abstract. The reviewer reproduced them from Table 1 as the mean relative gain over GameCraft Overall, FrontierSWE Dominance and ProgramBench pass rate; 82.86% is Pi's Dominance 35->64%. Dominance is a win rate against a pool that contains the HoH checkpoints themselves, and the paper does not explain the metric choice behind the aggregate.

claims.claim: Gains are not explained by more passes or more tokens alone.
claims.evidence: Table 2 (Codex/GPT-5.5, GameCraft only): at 1/2/3 passes HoH 59.71/64.84/71.52 vs Vanilla Continuation 49.58/54.99/58.24; HoH@2 (5.67M tokens) > Vanilla@3 (6.33M). A useful control, but only one configuration on one benchmark, and HoH@3 still uses more tokens (8.41M vs 6.33M).

claims.claim: Plan updates, evidence feedback and warm-start each contribute.
claims.evidence: Table 3 ablation (Codex, 45 GameCraft tasks): -8.13, -6.28, -7.85 points; w/o warm-start raises tokens 8.41M->11.12M. Single config, single run.

claims.claim: HoH autonomously builds a human-playable FPS over 70+ loops without human intervention.
claims.evidence: §5 case study with GPT-5.6-Sol: 81 issues recorded, 65 closed, 16 unresolved, 17 reopened. It uses extra domain tools (Godot MCP, asset generation skills) not used in the benchmarks. 'Human-playable', 'polished' and 'coherent storyline' are judged by the authors; there is no external player study.

patterns.note: Planner/developer/tester loop over existing harnesses beats one-pass and pass-matched continuation (Tables 1-2).
The tester's evidence fed back to the planner matters: removing evidence feedback costs 6.28 points (Table 3).
Artifacts exposed via a concise index with details retrieved on demand; role-scoped Markdown skills. Not ablated separately.
File-system project state and warm-start across loops; removing warm-start costs 7.85 points and 32% more tokens.
Role separation with independent testing; evidence comes from the full-system comparison rather than an isolated ablation of roles.
Versioned per-role, per-iteration history committed to GitHub enables rollback and traceability (case study).
Tokens reported per configuration; no budget mechanism.
Case study is driven by a PRD with player-observable acceptance criteria.

methodology.sample: GameCraft-Bench 45/140 tasks (stratified, seed fixed), FrontierSWE 15/17 tasks, ProgramBench (task count in supplement); one 70-loop case study.
methodology.baselines: Vanilla one-pass runs of the same harness+model; Vanilla Continuation (pass-matched) for Codex on GameCraft only. No comparison against other meta-harnesses or multi-agent frameworks.
methodology.models: GPT-5.5 (high) via Codex CLI 0.142.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro via OpenCode 1.14.30, MiniMax-M3 via Pi 0.80.10; GPT-5.6-Sol for the case study.
methodology.variance: One run per task-condition; no generation seed (App. B.2); 95% bootstrap CIs over tasks (Fig. 4), ±1 SE on FrontierSWE (Fig. 5).
methodology.ablations: w/o plan update, w/o evidence feedback, w/o warm-start (Codex, GameCraft).
methodology.contamination_controls: Evaluator outputs not returned to the development loop; private rubrics hidden from agents (appendix). No other contamination control.
methodology.languages: Godot/GDScript games, FrontierSWE and ProgramBench repos (languages not summarised in main text); no Java-specific evaluation.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; comment gives GitHub and project page only.
standards.artifacts: GitHub Flesymeb/HarnessOfHarness and project page; case-study repo with commit/issue history; supplementary task lists.

biases.detail: Authors evaluate their own framework; the case-study quality judgments ('polished visuals', 'human-playable') are their own.
Single run per condition with no generation seeds; CIs only over tasks.
Headline Table 1 compares 3 passes to 1; the pass-matched control covers only Codex on GameCraft.
The 52.25%/82.86% headline mixes metrics and leans on Dominance, a relative win rate within a pool that includes HoH checkpoints.
Qualitative Figure 6 and the FPS case show selected artifacts.
'Without human intervention', 'polished', 'complete' for a case that ends with 16 open and 17 reopened issues.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Third-party harnesses (Codex, OpenCode, Pi) and models (GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3) used as substrates; HoH is the authors' own system.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding section found.
coi.detail: Research lab evaluating its own open-source framework on third-party benchmarks; no commercial product promoted.

verdict_reason: Three harness-model pairs, three external benchmarks, a pass-matched control and ablations make this more rigorous than most harness papers, and the code is released. But each condition is a single run, the headline aggregate leans on a self-referential Dominance metric, the compute control is narrow, the case-study claims are self-judged, and there is no limitations section.
applicability: The most transferable design in this batch for a mixed-host team. HoH sits above existing CLIs (Codex, OpenCode, Pi) and works with three hosts and models, which matches the 'qr is not locked to a host' stance. A Java team could run a planner -> developer -> independent tester loop where each role must emit a schema-validated artifact (plan, change report, test evidence pack), with the tester's black-box checks running against the delivery APIs rather than the developer's own unit tests. Persist state on disk with an index (plans, issue table, evidence) instead of a memory service, and keep warm-start from the previous increment. The ablations suggest evidence-conditioned replanning and warm-start are worth implementing first. Caveats: the evidence is for greenfield single-repo game and program builds, not changes to ≥4 existing repositories with cross-repo contracts. Healthcare-education content has correctness and compliance criteria a self-run tester cannot certify, so keep human acceptance gates. Budget for about 3x the tokens of a single pass.

conflicts_with.detail: That paper finds self-authored verification unreliable in self-improving loops. HoH's internal tester is also agent-authored; HoH mitigates this by scoring with external evaluators that are hidden from the loop, but its own deployment-time QA has no sealed check.
